nameStory: The scientific name 'noxiosus' means 'harmful' or 'noxious' in Latin, though this tiny jumping spider poses no real threat to humans. The name might refer to its role as a predator of small insects, or perhaps early taxonomists were being dramatic about this diminutive hunter's fierce hunting style.
description: This is a small jumping spider with the characteristic compact, robust body typical of the family. Like all jumping spiders, it has excellent vision and hunts by stalking and pouncing on prey rather than building webs. These spiders are quite small, typically measuring just a few millimeters in body length. Their movements are quick and jerky, with the ability to leap several times their body length when hunting or escaping danger.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large forward-facing eyes arranged in a row across the front of the head, with the two middle eyes noticeably larger and giving it an almost cute, curious expression

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, chunky build with a relatively flat, rectangular front section (cephalothorax) that feels firm to the touch if gently handled

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, stop-and-go motions, often turning its entire body to look at you with those big front eyes, like a tiny eight-legged cat

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small spider, with the body typically smaller than your pinky nail and legs that don't extend much beyond a dime's width

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No hunting web, but creates small silk retreats that feel like tiny silk pouches under bark, stones, or in crevices

habitat: Look for this jumping spider in a variety of outdoor habitats including gardens, forest edges, and areas with mixed vegetation. They often hunt on plant surfaces, tree bark, and around human structures like fences and building exteriors. These spiders prefer areas with good sun exposure where they can warm themselves while hunting for small flying insects.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter shelters to hunt and mate. Look for them sunning themselves on warm surfaces during mild spring days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen hunting during daylight hours. Females may be found guarding small silk egg sacs in protected locations.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue hunting to build energy reserves before winter. Mated females focus on finding secure overwintering sites under bark or in building crevices.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, sheltering in silk-lined retreats under bark, stones, or in protected building crevices where they remain until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Jumping spiders can see in color and have vision quality that rivals that of much larger animals - they can spot and track prey from distances up to 20 times their body length, which would be like you clearly seeing a basketball from nearly a quarter mile away!
confusionNotes: With only one confirmed observation in New England, this species might be confused with other small jumping spiders in the region. The key is those four prominent front eyes in a straight row - if you see a tiny spider that seems to be 'looking' right back at you with big forward-facing eyes, you're likely dealing with a jumping spider of some kind.
contextualKnowledge: This species appears to be quite rare in New England, with only a single recorded observation in the region. It's possible that it's either at the northern edge of its range here or that it's simply overlooked due to its small size and similarity to other jumping spiders.
compareHints: This species is distinguished from its close relative, the Palaearctic Antmimic Jumping Spider (Synageles venator), primarily by geographic distribution and subtle differences in body proportions. Since both species are quite rare in New England, any small jumping spider you encounter is more likely to be one of the more common regional species like bold jumpers or zebra spiders, which are generally larger and more distinctively marked.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative Synageles noxiosus, the Palaearctic Antmimic tends to be more consistently dark in coloration and slightly more elongated in body shape.
